bib.title: Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities

question: Can the collective expertise of several LLMs be combined, through layered prompting alone, into a response better than any single LLM produces?
hypothesis: Integrating diverse perspectives from various models yields better responses than a single model, because LLMs are 'collaborative': they answer better when shown other models' outputs, even weaker ones.
contributions: Mixture-of-Agents framework leveraging multiple LLMs in layers
State-of-the-art performance on AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench and FLASK

method.summary: Layered MoA: each layer has n LLM agents; each agent in layer i+1 receives the original prompt plus all layer-i outputs wrapped in an Aggregate-and-Synthesize prompt. A single LLM in the last layer produces the final output. No fine-tuning; prompting only. Evaluated on AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench, FLASK with open-source proposers served via Together Inference Endpoint.
method.task: open-ended instruction following / chat response quality (plus MATH in appendix)

datasets.name: MATH
datasets.split: appendix D; subset size not stated

prompts.text:
You have been provided with a set of responses from various open-source models to the latest user query. Your task is to synthesize these responses into a single, high-quality response. It is crucial to critically evaluate the information provided in these responses, recognizing that some of it may be biased or incorrect. Your response should not simply replicate the given answers but should offer a refined, accurate, and comprehensive reply to the instruction. Ensure your response is well-structured, coherent, and adheres to the highest standards of accuracy and reliability.
Responses from models:
1. [Model Response from Ai,1]
2. [Model Response from Ai,2]
...
n. [Model Response from Ai,n]

You are a highly efficient assistant, who evaluates and selects the best large language model (LLMs) based on the quality of their responses to a given instruction. (Remainder, Appendix Table 5: instruction, six model outputs with identifiers; answer only with the best model identifier.)

limits: Authors: iterative aggregation means no first token until the last layer, high Time to First Token; suggest limiting layers (first aggregation gives the largest boost) or chunk-wise aggregation.
Number of proposers 'monotonic' claim is not strictly supported by Table 3 (n=2 58.8 > n=3 58.0).
Inconsistent headline: abstract 65.1% and intro 65.8%, Table 2 65.7 (GPT-4o variant).
Quality judged by GPT-4-based evaluator (AlpacaEval LC, MT-Bench); no human evaluation; the baseline reference in AlpacaEval is also GPT-4.
Cost uses API list prices (May 22, 2024) and GPT-4 tflops uses a rumored 8x220B size; latency is proxied by tflops, not measured.
MoA uses many calls: 6 proposers x 3 layers plus aggregator; compute cost per query far above a single model; MT-Bench gains marginal.
No sampling parameters (other than 0.7 in one ablation), max tokens or seeds given; MATH subset size and prompt not stated.
Optimal MoA architecture left to future work: 'systematic optimization of MoA architecture is an interesting direction'.

models proficient in synthesizing responses from other models into a single, high-quality output
